title: Why is Venice so wet?
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain why Venice floods and sinks. They cover the city's layout as about 124 islands linked by canals and bridges, its tidal lagoon and the sewage that flushes out with the tides, and rising sea levels that have increased flooding (aqua alta). They discuss subsidence from groundwater extraction, drilling and boat traffic, salt damage to brick from capillary action, and the building engineering that keeps structures intact. The main focus is the MOSE project, a set of hinged, air-filled steel gates across the three lagoon inlets, its cost, delays, corruption accusations, and criticisms such as possible sediment buildup and gate height. The episode closes with listener mail about a coffee shop worker who once served a man later revealed as a murderer, and sign-off material promoting a Venice documentary video and related articles.

segments.title: Morning-style intro and Italian banter
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about doing the episode in a morning style and about rising sea levels from climate change, noting Venice as a city facing the problem.

segments.title: Venice's shrinking population and frequent floods
segments.summary: Venice's population has fallen to about sixty people from about 180. The city used to flood about ten times a year and now faces far more floods, with water reaching knee height in places like San Marco Square.

segments.title: Antiquated sewage system and tourists in floodwater
segments.summary: Venice's sewer pipes empty into the canals, with some septic tanks added. Tides flush waste out to sea twice a day, but floods bring raw sewage into streets and tourists wade through it.

segments.title: Venice's layout: islands, canals and lagoon
segments.summary: Venice is described as about 124 small islands connected by 183 canals and bridges. It formed as separate neighborhoods for protection in a lagoon fed by three inlets where tides move water in and out.

segments.title: Causes of Venice's sinking and brick damage
segments.summary: Venice is sinking because of groundwater extraction, nearby drilling, and boat wakes eroding foundations. Salt water rises through brick by capillary action and crystallizes, cracking brickwork. Sediment buildup in canals is also a problem.

segments.title: Venice's ingenious building construction
segments.summary: Hosts describe wall hooks, roof caps that hold walls in, flexible interior walls, and wooden piles beneath buildings, drawn from the Venice Backstage video.

segments.title: The MOSE flood barrier explained
segments.summary: The MOSE project uses hinged steel gates in trenches across the three lagoon inlets. They are filled with air to rise and block high tides, and the name also refers to Moses. Construction began in 2003 after years of planning.

segments.title: MOSE costs, corruption, and criticisms
segments.summary: The project was estimated at two to three billion dollars and is over budget and behind schedule. There were corruption accusations, a first successful test in 2012, and tracking for 2016. Critics raise sea level, sediment, environmental, and Netherlands-style alternative concerns.

segments.title: Listener mail: ice cream and a murderer
segments.summary: A listener recounts serving ice cream to a man who later was revealed as a murderer, connecting it to the insanity defense episode.

segments.title: Sign-off and Venice video plug
segments.summary: Hosts recommend the Venice Backstage video, point to the website, and sign off.
